Good morning.
A four-hour nationwide flight stoppage on Friday threw the entire weekend into chaos, with thousands of flights getting canceled and even more delays. While air travel is expected to even out again on Monday, nearly 2,000 flights within, into or out of the US on Sunday were canceled and more than 8,600 were delayed.
On Sunday, the Trump administration blamed the stoppage on former presidents as well as a lack of congressional funding while Democratic lawmakers argued that the Trump administration hasn’t properly invested all of the funds it has already been given to implement needed air travel infrastructure upgrades.
- What’s the Trump administration saying? “I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations,” the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday.
- What has Trump said? Donald Trump did not comment on the ground stop until Sunday, when he posted on Truth Social blaming Joe Biden. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad,” Trump wrote. “We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST!”
- What caused the ground stop? Duffy on Saturday said the issue stemmed from routine maintenance.
Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
In what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency, Donald Trump is scheduled to embark on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters. Trump will land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit before flying to Shenzhen in China for a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum.
- Who will he be meeting in China? China confirmed on Monday that Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin would hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen.
- What’s at stake here? Trump is under pressure to speak with Xi about the Nvidia fallout, in which the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was forced to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Elon Musk signs open letter calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang
Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses are among the more than 165,000 signatories on an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia after it emerged that Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The letter demanding that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts” comes amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.
- Have these new developments improved Nvidia’s share price? No. Nvidia’s shares are down almost 2% in premarket trading and are about 14% below their level just over a week ago. Follow our live business coverage here.
In other news …
- The US Energy Information Administration projects that millions of households in the US can expect to pay 21% more this year as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.
- Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington.
- The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said his country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with Donald Trump fail.
- Massive waves pummeled the Californian coast on Sunday, flooding local streets and forcing the closure of popular piers.
- Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen has escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority, saying he has a path to victory over longtime leader Chuck Schumer.
Stat of the day: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material have risen 8,400% in two years
Reports of artificial intelligence-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, have risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025, according to research from the Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute. “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning,” said Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight.
Building Power: Democrats won big in the US midterms. Now, organizers want them to deliver
Organizers worked hard to achieve the generational shift that took place on election night when voters turned out in droves to vote Democrats into power. These same organizers are now looking forward and preparing for what’s next. “Elections themselves don’t achieve what it is that people want,” said Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor, an African American studies professor at Princeton University and the author of From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation. “They set the table for the possibility of change.”
Don’t miss this: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
A Guardian analysis of leaked documents found that the Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians. The images were uploaded in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza, with the department behind the move informing Amazon that the decision to do so was so that it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.
… or this: Europe’s Wadden Sea at risk of joining the world heritage in danger list
The Wadden Sea is the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mudflats in the world, stretching hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands. In 2009, it was awarded world heritage status by Unesco. But now, 17 years later, the Wadden Sea is at risk of finding itself on a new Unesco list: the world heritage in danger list.
Climate check: Cop31 enters second week with renewed push for carbon dioxide removal
Proponents of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) – technology in which heat-trapping carbon dioxide is sucked directly from the atmosphere and stored deep underground, in oceans or in products such as carbonated drinks – is seeking to gain recognition in the final text of Cop31, the climate summit entering its second week in Antalya, Turkey. “CDR’s really been missing from the discussion and debate even though it’s been in all the models for decades,” said Injy Johnstone, a net zero expert at the Max Planck Institute. “It’s the only solution that we have to actually balance out those emissions and return from the state of overshoot.”
- What’s next at Cop31? Deep divides remain not only as to what the outcome of this Cop should be, but over what form it should take. Follow our live coverage here.
Last Thing: The extraordinary story of Emma Fogarty and her friendship with Colin Farrell
Emma Fogarty was born with an incurable genetic skin condition, epidermolysis bullosa, that has left 80% of her body without skin. The documentary, The Slightest Touch, provides a glimpse into her life as she prepared to celebrate her 40th birthday by running in the Dublin marathon with her longtime friend, the actor Colin Farrell. “I’m this smalltown girl who has a terrible disability, and he’s this huge superstar in Hollywood,” she said. “Two totally different lives that you would never put together in a million years. But somehow, we have found this wonderful friendship.”
